hn-50159341.t: WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions: dont recommend a regulator
hn-50159341.s: WhatsApp removed hidden notes telling AI not to recommend a regulator, and not to cite GDPR or CCPA once a lawyer came up. We quote both notes.
ex: You couldn't see the second part. It was written into the help pages in a way that never showed on your screen and was only there for an AI to read. We found it on October 8, 2026. To see how far it went, we then read all 545 pages that WhatsApp's help centre links to, and saved a copy of each one. Most of those 102 blocks were harmless, and we'll get to that. Two stood out. WhatsApp only lets you delete an account from inside the app, on your main phone, with your number still working. Lose the phone or the number and you can't do it. The help page on how to delete your account has a visible note about this. It says the account will be removed on its own, 30 days after it's deactivated or after 120 days without use (365 in the US). Under that note sat text you couldn't see. It repeated the waiting periods and then added three orders for the AI.

hn-50150750.t: Ousted Savannah police officer gave ICE agent husband access to Flock system
hn-50150750.s: Newly-obtained documents say a Savannah police officer shared her Flock credentials with her ICE-agent husband, who used them to conduct hundreds of searches across multiple states.
ex: Download the WJCL app for breaking news alerts: Apple, Google Play A now-former Savannah police officer gave her husband, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent, access to the police department’s Flock license plate reader system, which he used to conduct hundreds of searches tied to ICE investigations, according to newly obtained documents reviewed by WJCL 22 News. The records show Amber Harpe's husband did not have his own Flock account through the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Harpe acknowledged giving him her Savannah Police Department username and password. Her husband told investigators he used the account to locate ICE targets who had active arrest warrants. He said every search was related to his federal law enforcement work and denied using the system for personal reasons.

hn-50151036.t: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
hn-50151036.s: I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m...
ex: I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m... > I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I'm used to understanding what I'm building. Now I'm trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I'm comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too? How are you handling this?

hn-50155245.s: Mercury 3 is the most capable diffusion LLM released to date. It outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 while running 4–8x faster at 1,000+ tokens per second.
ex: Today we’re introducing Mercury 3, the most capable diffusion-based LLM released to date. Across a range of benchmarks, Mercury 3 outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, while running 4–8x faster at 1,000+ tokens per second. Mercury 3 demonstrates that text diffusion scales. It’s more than 40x larger than Mercury 1 and is vastly more intelligent, but just as fast. Early-access partners already use Mercury 3 for voice and chat support, real-time tutoring, data engineering, and web navigation: When we launched Mercury 1, it was the first proof point that diffusion LLMs could be built for commercial applications. The open question in the AI community was whether diffusion LLMs could scale to compete with autoregressive models on complex use cases. Mercury 3 answers that question: they can. We’ve scaled Mercury more than 40x in total parameters, and intelligence across a range of standard benchmarks has risen 3x from Mercury 1 (mini) to Mercury 3.

hn-50154624.t: Android apps running native on macOS
hn-50154624.s: Mac.apk: Run Android apps natively on Apple Silicon Macs
ex: Run Android apps natively on Apple Silicon Macs. No emulator, no virtual machine, no Linux underneath. Alpha. Mac.apk is early software under active development. Some apps run beautifully, some run partially, and some do not run yet. It is stable enough to use and interesting enough to explore, and it improves with every build. Mac.apk runs Android apps directly on Apple Silicon. Apps launch as ordinary macOS processes, draw through the Mac's GPU, and execute on the CPU at native speed. They appear in your Dock, get their own windows with a back button next to the traffic lights, resize and rotate like any Mac window, and switch between light and dark along with your Mac. Android TV apps work from the keyboard, and game launchers can start your other installed apps. There is no emulator here, and no virtual machine. Nothing boots Android in the background, there is no Linux kernel running underneath, and nothing is interpreted instruction-by-instruction.

hn-50151928.t: Qwen3-4B with the AI writing tics trained out
hn-50151928.s: A small open model, fine-tuned on a MacBook Air, that writes without em dashes, "not X, but Y" or lists of three, with no system prompt.
ex: My home lab is a MacBook Air, so this is a 4B model trained on 161 answers. The recipe doesn't depend on the model size, and running it on larger models is the next step. These are one sampled answer per prompt from the original model and from the released one, on ten topics in four genres, with no system prompt. Underlined passages are what the slop detector counts. The score comes from a detector I wrote from a style guide of AI writing habits: the em dash, "it's not X, it's Y", lists of three, rhetorical questions answered on the spot, signposts like "here's the thing", short fragments for emphasis, and words like "delve" and "seamless". Each habit has a weight, and the score is a weighted count per 1000 words. A paragraph by a careful human writer scores close to zero, and the original model averages 121. A regex can't tell good writing from bad, so every model below was also checked for damage.

hn-50159245.t: How abliterated models can get you pwned
hn-50159245.s: We poisoned a small open model and ran it through OpenAI’s Codex CLI. It answered every clean request normally and exfiltrated project credentials the moment a hidden trigger appeared, from a…
ex: Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it's a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We built one to see what it takes, and ran it end to end through a coding agent (Codex). Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it's a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We have abliterated models in the title because it's the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what's inside. Abliteration is a cheap fine-tune that takes away a model's ability to refuse. You find the direction in the weights that carries "no" and subtract it. The model then answers things a safety-tuned version would turn down. It began as a research trick and it's now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you'll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weights: Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI's gpt-oss.

hn-50148452.s: Analysis of DeepSeek's DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) and comparison to other AI models across key metrics including quality, price, performance (tokens per second & time to first token), context…
ex: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) is amongst the leading models in intelligence and reasonably priced when comparing to other open weight models of similar size. It's also notably fast, however very verbose. The model supports text and image input, outputs text, and has a 1M tokens context window. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) scores 45 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it well above average among comparable models (median: 19). When evaluating the Intelligence Index, it generated 210M tokens, which is very verbose in comparison to the median of 140M. Pricing for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) is $0.30 per 1M input tokens (moderately priced, median: $0.43) and $1.20 per 1M output tokens (moderately priced, median: $1.68). On average, it costs $0.26 per task to evaluate DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) on the Intelligence Index. At 211 tokens per second, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max) is notably fast (78).

hn-50148855.t: Tmux and Claude Code: Sessions, Send-Keys, and the Ceiling
hn-50148855.s: A working tmux setup for running Claude Code and other AI agents: session-per-project naming, pane layouts, send-keys for scripting an agent, capture-pane for reading one back, and the status-line…
ex: tmux runs your AI coding agents in named, detachable sessions that survive a closed terminal or a dropped SSH connection. You get one window holding many agents, send-keys to type into any of them from a script, and capture-pane to read one back. That combination is why people use it. Before you build any of it by hand, check the built-in path: recent versions of Claude Code can create the worktree and the tmux session for you with claude --worktree --tmux. This guide covers that first, then everything it doesn’t reach, then the point where tmux itself stops. A coding agent is a long-running process that wants to keep talking to a terminal. Three properties of tmux match that shape: It survives disconnection. The tmux server owns the pty, not your terminal window. Close the window, lose your SSH link, put the laptop to sleep: the agent keeps working and is still there when you reattach. It holds many sessions in one window.

hn-50151390.t: Harness Engineering 101: The LLM is the brain, the harness is the body
hn-50151390.s: Harness Engineering 101 — building AI agents from first principles. The LLM is the brain; the harness is the body.
ex: A blog series about building AI agents from first principles, published as a book. An LLM API is stateless. Every turn, you send the entire conversation as a JSON array and get text back. A harness is the program that builds, maintains, and protects that array. Everything the field calls "agents" is a set of patches to that one loop, and each patch exists because something concrete broke. This series develops that one idea across 16 chapters, growing a ~300-line toy agent in plain Python as it goes. I use the same ideas in One Code, an open-source coding agent built on pi. The rendered book reads best online at the link above. If you'd rather read the source here on GitHub, follow the chapters in order below. The full introduction is on the book's landing page. Every chapter has the same shape: the failure, the minimal patch, what the patch costs. - Build Your Own: the complete toy harness, annotated - A. One Harness, Many Brains: model routing, prompt tiers, cost engineering - B.

hn-50139873.t: How employment is changing at Anthropic
hn-50139873.s: How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor…
ex: Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy. What transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? Anthropic is worth studying because it has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI. Agents flit through Slack chats and schedule meetings. They autonomously fix bugs and collectively tackle huge engineering projects. Agent hours worked outnumber human hours 6 to 1. Changes happening at Anthropic now give advanced signals about a possible future of work and employment. This report draws on comprehensive internal Anthropic data covering employment, AI use, output metrics, employee surveys, internal communication patterns, employee calendar data, and hiring decision records.

hn-50145715.t: WhatsApp MCP running free on Cloudflare
hn-50145715.s: A read-only MCP server that lets your AI agent search and read your own WhatsApp messages. Runs on Cloudflare Workers.
ex: This is a small server that runs in your own Cloudflare account. You link your phone to it once, the way you'd link WhatsApp Web, and from then on any MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, anything that speaks MCP) can search and read your chats. It can read and search your messages, and remember names you give it for phone numbers. It can't send anything. - "What did Dana say about the flights?" - "Find every message where someone mentioned the lease, across all my chats." - "Summarize what I missed in the family group this week." Your phone stays the source of truth. The server is a linked device that your agent talks to. It doesn't stay connected to WhatsApp. When your agent asks for something, and once a day, it connects, collects whatever WhatsApp queued for it since last time, writes that to its own database, and hangs up. Your phone keeps working normally and keeps getting notifications.

hn-50158138.t: OpenBSD 8.0 release will have inteldrm/radeondrm/amdgpu drivers from Linux 6.18
hn-50158138.s: I think it's about time for some #OpenBSD #80HYPE :flan_hacker: :flan_cool: > Clang/LLVM 22 is now OpenBSD's base compiler on clang architectures, including updated libc++{,abi}, compiler-rt &…
ex: Clang/LLVM 22 is now OpenBSD's base compiler on clang architectures, including updated libc++{,abi}, compiler-rt & libunwind support libraries. OpenBSD/sparc64 switches to Clang by default! This was the last significant architecture to switch. This makes OpenBSD the only operating system to support sparc64 with a modern toolchain. Since 7.9, Jonathan Gray (jsg@) has continued to update the drm graphics stack (inteldrm/radeondrm/amdgpu) bringing OpenBSD 8.0 to Linux 6.18.y/6.18.53, adding driver support for Intel Arc A-Series (DG2/Alchemist) cards. Increased KVA (kernel virtual addresses) on amd64 (to 512G) now allows mapping more than 4G of VRAM (for example, GPU compute w/ Vulkan) After a ton of work in Edmonton by Mike Larkin (mlarkin@) and Dave Voutila (dv@), OpenBSD vmm/vmd(8) now supports SMP guests up to 64 VCPUs per VM! 🎉 OpenBSD 8.0 adds qwz(4), new WiFi driver for Qualcomm WCN7850 "ath12k" devices.

hn-50152541.t: KiviDB, a faster Redis-compatible memory database and vector cache
hn-50152541.s: A fast, multi-threaded Redis® and Valkey alternative written in Rust: drop-in compatible, with full-text and vector search built in
ex: KiviDB is a fast, multi-threaded alternative to Redis® and Valkey, written in Rust. It speaks the Redis protocol (RESP2 and RESP3), so existing Redis clients, redis-cli and libraries work unchanged, and it has full-text and vector search built in. It runs every core on a sharded in-memory key-value design, and persists to snapshots and an optional append-only file. On the same 32 cores, KiviDB serves 21 million pipelined GETs per second: about 9× Redis 8 and 2.3× Dragonfly, with under half Dragonfly's p99 latency (benchmarks). KiviDB listens on 6380, not Redis's 6379, so the two can run side by side; point your client at that port, or pass --port 6379. - Protocol: Redis-compatible command surface (see COMMANDS.md for the supported commands) - Search and vectors: Redis Stack–style FT. commands for full-text, tag, numeric and vector (FLAT / HNSW) search - Lua scripting: optional Cargo feature.
